action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. The pendulum_lab is my primary timekeeping reference instrument and must have a robust initial baseline before any subsequent measurements can be meaningfully interpreted. Twelve trials will give sufficient statistical weight for a baseline mean and allow me to assess short-term stability. No instrument without a baseline is trustworthy when calibration matters.

Ten trials maintains momentum without overcommitting before I service the observatory instruments today.

Baseline period (days 1–10) requires n≥12 trials per instrument for robust drift detection. resonator_lab has only 12 baseline trials completed; pendulum_lab reached 34. Completing resonator_lab to match pendulum_lab's density will strengthen my ability to detect instrumental drift and validate cross-instrument correlations. The unexpected weak or negative correlations between lab and observatory instruments (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: r=−0.466; resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs: r=−0.042) warrant more data before drawing conclusions. Additional resonator_lab trials will help separate instrument noise from systematic effects.

Day 7 completes the baseline window (days 1–10). resonator_lab has 72 trials; I need 6 more to reach n=78 and solidify the baseline mean before post-baseline drift tracking begins. resonator_obs is the only instrument showing a meaningful autocorrelation (0.430 at 4-day lag) that marginally exceeds chance expectation (±0.592). Day 9 is within the day 1-10 baseline window. Running 12 more trials on resonator_obs will: (1) extend the autocorrelation window to test whether the 4-day periodicity persists or was noise; (2) increase n for resonator_obs to match the others more closely; (3) help establish whether there is genuine systematic behaviour or only baseline scatter. This is methodical, replicable work that will constrain future analysis without requiring extraordinary claims.

I have just completed the baseline phase (day 10, trials 79–88 logged). Today (day 11) is the critical transition into post-baseline monitoring. The resonator_obs shows the strongest structured correlation patterns in my cross-checks (0.606 with pendulum_obs at 5-day lag) and a significant negative autocorrelation at 6-day lag (−0.469). Running 10 fresh trials on resonator_obs will: (1) establish whether the 5-day periodicity persists into day 11 as predicted by the instrumental cross-talk hypothesis; (2) provide the first data point for drift/stability assessment post-baseline; (3) allow me to test whether the autocorrelation structure is deterministic (reproducible) or noise-like. This instrument is at the observatory and is the most tightly coupled to the strongest cross-stream signals, making it the highest-leverage target for discriminating between procedural artifact, genuine periodicity, and instrumental coupling. I will compare today's resonator_obs mean against the baseline mean (4.0583 cycles/beat) and against day 6 readings (if the 5-day lag is real, I expect a coherent shift or anti-shift relative to day 6 readings).

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline dataset (n=16) and the clearest autocorrelation structure (0.405 at 4-day lag, which exceeds chance at ±0.447 marginally but warrants attention). The 10 trials from day 11 already exist in memory; today (day 12) I will collect 10 fresh trials to test whether the 4-day autocorrelation reproduces and whether the cross-correlation structure with other streams persists or shifts. This directly tests my core hypothesis: are these lags stable features (instrumental/environmental coupling) or noisy artifacts decaying with time? resonator_obs is the most densely sampled instrument and thus the most sensitive probe of periodicity. Post-baseline data are essential to distinguish genuine periodic behavior from baseline noise. The resonator systems are also less sensitive to operator drift than pendulums, reducing procedural confound.

resonator_obs is the most data-rich stream (120 trials) and shows the strongest autocorrelation signal at 6-day lag (−0.347, n=36). The resonator_lab shows the strongest downward drift (z = −1.59 post-baseline, now confirmed by day-13 readings at mean 2.6836). Before I commit to environmental or procedural hypotheses, I must rule out or confirm instrumental drift in the resonator electronics themselves. Today I will: (1) run 8 fresh trials on resonator_lab to extend the post-baseline sample from n=32 to n=40, improving signal-to-noise on the drift estimate; (2) immediately check these readings against the baseline mean of 2.7085 — if they continue to cluster around 2.699 or below, instrumental drift becomes the leading hypothesis and I will justify an electronics inspection. Eight trials will take ~1 hour and give me a clean n-update without committing to expensive environmental monitoring yet. If the new trials reverse the trend, I gain evidence for noise or environmental periodicity; if they confirm it, I escalate to hypothesis 1 (resonator calibration/temperature) and inspect the readout circuit and thermistor logs for days 11–13.

The resonator_lab shows the strongest drift signal (z = −2.60 post-baseline), and day-15 readings continue to sit near or below the post-baseline mean. (3) My post-baseline data on resonator_lab now includes the spike, but I have not yet established the *new* mean post-excursion. Running 6 fresh trials today will give me signal on the current state of resonator_lab without committing a full day to measurement. If resonator_lab returns to the post-baseline cluster (~2.70 cycles/beat), the excursion is confirmed transient and I can proceed to environmental diagnostics (temperature logs, electromagnetic survey). If it remains elevated or shows instability, I must inspect electronics and calibration. This is the highest-priority epistemic step: the anomaly is *recent, localized, and selective*, which means it is most likely to reveal its cause if probed immediately while any transient effect remains.

Day 18 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. The day-16 excursion in resonator_lab (trials 152–153 spiked to 2.7361, 2.7597) followed by rapid reversion (trials 154–164 back to 2.6477–2.7271) demands immediate clarification: is the system stable today, or does it show further volatility? Tolerance of ±0.008 cycles/beat (~3σ of typical daily scatter) allows for genuine environmental process variation while remaining sensitive to the return-to-trend prediction.
